review:
[h1] Such potential lasting so short is a complete disappointment. [/h1]

[h2] Story and Characters [/h2]

RE3 tells the struggle of S.T.A.R.S member and our main protagonist, Jill Valentine, trying to escape the biological disaster Umbrella unleashed on the city. Carlos Oliveira, whom we encounter along this journey, helps us. If you ask me, he turned out to be quite a naive and honest character. Just like Carlos, Jill trusts people way too quickly, and this creates some issues for us. The story generally stays faithful to the original game, but the narrative pacing is also quite fast. Because it isn't as long and detailed as RE2, it unfortunately left an unfinished feeling for me. On my first playthrough, exploring around, I finished the game in nearly 3-4 hours, which I think is quite short.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails?id=3677893413
As can be understood from the title of the original game, the main boss in this REMAKE is once again NEMESIS. In my opinion, it would have been better if the game's title remained the same as the old one. Nemesis adds tension to the story from the very beginning of the game. Him suddenly popping up in front of us and being difficult to take down gives us moments of instant panic.

[h2] Graphics and Atmosphere [/h2]

The graphics are successful. The level of detail, character models, and lighting are quite impressive. CAPCOM does this REMAKE thing well. Especially the night atmosphere and the ruined city design we remember from RE2 reflect the dark tone of the game very well. The hospital section and indoor areas keep the feeling of tension alive. The atmosphere is generally set up very well. There is an ambiance that keeps us constantly on alert.

[h2] Technical and Performance [/h2]

While playing at 2K resolution and Ultra settings, it hovered around 130-140 FPS on average, which surprised me quite a bit. The game has an optimization that shouldn't be underestimated. The RE Engine runs very stably.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails?id=3677540577
[h2] Music and Sound Effects [/h2]

Background music is designed to support the atmosphere. Especially during moments of tension, the music swells and ramps up the suspense. One of the biggest reasons we feel like something is about to happen at any second is the music. Even hearing Nemesis' footsteps from a distance is an element of tension on its own.

[h2] Gameplay and Mechanics [/h2]

Most of us know that we don't play the remade titles in the Resident Evil series for their story. Yes, even if we learn the story more or less, most of us play for the characters and gameplay. Just like in RE2, there is fluid gameplay. Hit feedback and gunplay are solid. The dodge mechanic and the short-term buff it provides afterward are well thought out for shootouts. Fights against Nemesis turned out great, both visually and gameplay-wise. We also shouldn't forget: do not expect puzzles like RE2 from this game. The scarcity of puzzles and keeping certain sections short might make it feel a bit lacking compared to the classic Resident Evil experience. Although the original game was great and gripping for its time, the REMAKE version falls a bit below the bar for today's standards.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails?id=3677868771
[h2] Overall [/h2]

RE3 offers a strong, concise experience with its atmosphere, graphics, and gameplay. The action dose is high, the pacing is fast, and having a boss like Nemesis is impressive. But as I said above, being shallow makes you feel that it didn't utilize the game's potential to the fullest. At the very least, they could have added sections that fit the original game without feeling out of place. We also shouldn't forget that it is a game built on the foundations of RE2.

It's difficult to review this game without mentioning the RE2 remake, so I won't fight it. Compared to RE2, this game is very disappointing. RE2 started with the original game, built on it, modernized it, and made a definitive version that fits very well with what gamers expect nowadays, whilst still maintaining the spirit of the original.

RE3 did the opposite. It wasn't very close to the original at all except for the basic premise. The story was different, the game route was different, MANY areas and bosses were cut (at least a third to half of the original game), and ALL puzzles were cut. The only puzzles present could be solved by a child and they basically give you the solutions anyways. There isn't any survival horror left, it's just a third-person shooter. You get more than enough ammo on Standard difficulty to kill everything in your way.

I beat the game in 5 hours - and I was stopping to smell the roses. On top of being extremely short, there is basically no replayability either. Unlike RE2's Tyrant, this game's Nemesis is not dynamic. He shows up at the exact same places every time. In fact, the whole game is completely linear, with everything being the same every time. You can't even play as a different character or do a different route like in RE2. Once you've played it once, all there is to do is use points to buy helpful "boosts" in the in-game store, and play the same campaign over again.

The visuals, music, sound effects, and characters were all good. Gunplay still feels tight like in RE2, and you will be doing a lot more shooting in this game, so it's good that it holds up. The Hunter Beta is a good reimagining of a classic enemy. The Hunter Gamma is pretty terrible, and defeating it is more a measure of how well you can shoot a flame grenade into its mouth before getting insta-killed than anything else. The Drain Deimos is not at all threatening, except in the VERY distasteful and unnecessary scene where it throat-****s Jill.

All in all, the game is mediocre if you get it for $20 CDN / $15 USD. Do not buy it at full price. I have no doubt that the cutting of content and dumbing-down of gameplay was for the sake of finishing the multiplayer component. Nobody asked for that, and RE3 was - and still is - some RE fans' favourite in the whole series. I am very disappointed to see them treat the game this carelessly. They totally wasted the opportunity to remake a great game, most likely so they could push the microtransaction-riddled disaster that is RE: Resistance and make more money. Now there is no way RE3 fans will ever get to play a good remake.

RE2 shows how to remake a classic game the right way. RE3 shows how to do it the wrong way.

[h1] As a gamer I recommend it, as a resident evil fan I only feel disappointment :/  [/h1]

This game objectively is good/ ok-ish, but as a remake is really barebones and it lacks in so many ways in comparison with the original and with the remake of resident evil 2. I recommend people to buy it at a heavy discount but this is in no way a complete game, they decided to cut half of the game just to put a multiplayer mode call "RESISTANCE" that was already dead a month after release, Capcom keeps trying to make RE multiplayer games  with no idea of what people want, we want coop game, no call of duty or Dying light clones. Please stop, they ended up hurting the campaign just for the sake of it...

[u]  [b] The good stuff [/b] [/u] 

This game has good qualities to it, this is by no means a bad game (although it was a rip off at 60 dollars at launch so I didn't buy it at that price) so let's start. 

The voice acting is superb, specially Jill, I love seeing a "new game" with her as a protagonist again, I like her new design but I still like her old one a bit more but it's still great, although is sad to see is such a short game :/. Nemesis design is great too, and how racoon city looks is just breathtaking, gameplay is very similar to RE2 but is a bit faster thanks to Jill's new dodge technique. The game is overall fun and I liked it, there are certain story moments that are great but the more I look at it the cons start to pop up more than the pros sadly.

[u]  [b] The bad stuff: The game that it will never be [/b] [/u] 

The remake of this game cuts so many stuff from the original, no clocktower, no park, no exploration, no anticipation, almost no puzzles, no dismemberment system as RE2, and the list can go all day. RE3 remake is extremely linear, the game is filled with scripted moments that makes nemesis to not be a menace at all, in RE2 remake MR.X was a chasing menace made to kill every witness of the racoon city incident, chasing you across the RPD in such unexpected ways and it was terrifying. But in RE3 Nemesis only has 1 real persecutor segment and is stunned with a battery in the most lame way possible, the beast that is meant to kill all the STARS members to avoid spreading the information of the mansion incident, is now just a predictable enemy that doesn't chase you after the first 20 min  of the game.... this is not how is supposed to work and now makes sense why Nemesis is no longer on the title of the game.

The overall map of raccoon city is now limited to just 2 streets and like 3 hallways, this is supposed to be the Racoon city game, but the city segment is so short that is really sad, all the locations are there but they are just cameos  and references, so they are closed in one way or another as if it was a fan game instead of a AAA remake like RE2 was, and after this section nemesis won't chase you anymore because they rushed their "animal" form so quickly for the sake of action set pieces that is no longer menacing, he just becomes a boss everytime you see him :/. So the rocket launcher nemesis is basically limited to a 2 minute sequence... like why??? that is his signature  weapon and is now just a cameo for 5 seconds because is just a run segment so you don't even see him using it. So, going back to the map, now is just City => Sewers => Hospital => Lab and yeah RE2 only had 3.5 locations but all of them were connected via puzzles but in this one they are shorter, they are not connected, you just see them once.

They also completely eliminated the decision making of the original, making this 100% linear in level design and 100% linear in story too. Now you can't choose if you want to explore the city but you can't choose story elements either, so the replayability of this game is non existent. And it sucks because they touched the PTSD of Jill on the beginning of this game but just a little bit, and is such a miss opportunity because if they had included more nightmares and more story choices they could've made a really good exploration of her character, but after the intro she just becomes a bad ass character with no build up :(.

[u] [b] Conclusion [/b] [/u] 

I am negative overall but I actually enjoyed the game, but this game could've been such a masterpiece just as RE2 was, imagining a complete racoon city with interconnected puzzles with nemesis chasing you across all the city as MR.X did , making decisions in the game with multiple endings, giving STARS members more screen time and exploring how umbrella is chasing Jill and how she deals with it thanks to her PTSD and her lack of trust in others.  that is a game I imagined after finishing RE2 remake, and is obvious this game was not made by the same team. This was made by a different team at capcom and it really shows. The RE2 team is working on the RE4 remake so I am excited for that one. That's why I can't recommend it as an RE fan, Capcom gave this game, THE NEMESIS GAME, to a secondary group and took half of their resources to make a trash multiplayer game that was dead a week after release, the lack of time and love put in this proyect is shown if you compare it with RE2 or the original RE3. As a separate thing , yeah is good, is decent. But capcom just chased the easiest and laziest  way to make money, and it sucks this game will always be remembered as the game it will never be :'(.

Buy it at a heavy discount, I give it a thumbs down because the average steam score is now at 79% which is undeserved, for me is around the 70s, so I do it to compensate.

Resident Evil 3: Nemesis was the first Resident Evil game I ever played, so this entry has a special place in my heart. That’s why this remake was especially disappointing.
The game has great graphics, a good atmosphere, and fun gameplay, but the amount of content that was cut is way too aggressive. Entire areas from the original were removed, including Raccoon Park and the Clock Tower. Enemies such as the giant spiders and the Gravedigger were also completely cut.
The campaign is only around 3–4 hours long, depending on how you play, which is less than half the length of the original. They also removed the alternate endings, leaving a much more linear experience with less replay value.
And instead of adding more content, it feels like Capcom decided to spam Nemesis as many times as possible throughout the game. His constant appearances eventually become repetitive rather than exciting.
Honestly, this feels more like a DLC sold as a full remake than a complete remake of Resident Evil 3.
It really feels like Capcom wanted to milk this release for as much money as possible, putting out a half-finished product instead of taking the time to make a remake worthy of the original.
The graphics are great and the gameplay is fun, but that doesn't justify the huge amount of cut content or such a short campaign.
My recommendation: only buy it on sale. At full price, it's not worth it—6/10

[h1]A great game but a bad remake?[/h1]
[hr][/hr]

This seems to be the general consensus about this game.
[b]However[/b]... I disagree.

[hr][/hr]

RE3R has some good things going for it. Namely solid visuals overall and improved dodge mechanic compared to the original game.

The story in the original game always has been minimalistic, being all about surviving and escaping Raccoon City.  
Now I feel the Remake made unnecessary changes in the second half of the game regarding the protagonists' goals which severely dampens what the actual story is all about: [b]Survival[/b].

The 1999 game made use of a show, don't tell narration style.  
The Remake manages to convey less with more.

[hr][/hr]

The original game had four main locations to explore as you progressed through the game.

[list]
[*]Raccoon City's streets (including the R.P.D)
[*]The Clocktower
[*]The Park
[*]The Factory
[/list]

Out of those four. Only [b]ONE[/b] has been preserved.  
You'd think at least it would have been expanded?

[b]Well you'd be wrong[/b] as the opposite happened.  
Raccoon City streets feel so much smaller now.

Oh? New locations you say?

[b]The sewers![/b]  
An 8-minute adventure in a place that only exists for the sake of cutting corners and reusing assets from Resident Evil 2 Remake.

Oh the generic looking lab that is replacing the Factory as the game's final area?  
It looks strangely close to the laboratory from RE2R...

The short hospital section of the original game has been expanded a bit.  
It is a welcome addition but simply doesn't compensate for the loss of Clocktower or Park sections.

[hr][/hr]

[b]Now Nemesis.[/b]

The short build-up leading to its encounter is absent from the Remake as you'll meet him in the literal first 2 minutes of gameplay.

The then semi-dynamic stalker antagonist that oppressed you for the majority of the game, chasing you across rooms and taking away any semblance of solace you thought you had...

Well, it's a complete shadow of its former self now.

A lot of its encounters are scripted set pieces and the few times he's actually roaming around, he's a minor inconvenience that can be taken down with extreme ease.

Which in turn really lessens the forced boss battles with it.  
To think they had a good blueprint for a stalker type threat in RE2R.

[hr][/hr]

RE3R gameplay feels identical to RE2R with the addition of dodges.

Although, shooting zombies feels way less satisfying due to the lack of dynamic limb dismembering that you could use at your advantage in RE2R.

The zombies here feel more rigid and don't react as much to the lead you shoot in their flesh, which is a major let-down for a game that is mostly about shooting zombies when it comes to its gameplay.

[hr][/hr]

A lot of people complain RE3R is short.  
That is true.  
It was also true about the original game.

[b]However[/b] the Live Selection feature from the original game has been completely scrapped.  
It added some decision making that would change how the events of the game unfold.

The 1999 RE3 was slightly less linear too, the Remake plays more like a traditional TPS game where you simply press forward towards your next objective.

The RNG aspect of the original also has been ditched, affecting the ammo placement and also enemies placement and spawns.  
Those things added variance across multiple playthroughs thus increasing the replay value tremendously.

The higher unlockable difficulty modes in the Remake change some enemy and resource placement but in a fixed way though.

[hr][/hr]

The whole Mercenaries game mode has been cut as well in favour of Resident Evil Resistance, a trash multiplayer game which is its own can of worms at this point.

[hr][/hr]

[b]Other things didn't make the cut in RE3R:[/b]

[list]
[*]Several weapons missing.
[*]A whole boss encounter.
[*]Some minor enemies.
[*]Unlockable costumes. (More than 5 depending on game versions. Remake has 1 unlockable costume and 1 DLC costume)
[*]Numerous puzzles. (The Remake has 2 and barely requires any thought)
[*]The respect for the original material.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

Even trying my best to not compare the Remake to the 1999 original.

Everything that's left is a mediocre action game that doesn't manage to live up to the standards set by RE2R.

It's lazy in many aspects and an opportunistic release to make profit off the hype RE2R created.

[hr][/hr]

Compared to RE2R, this remake left me feeling a bit torn. On one hand, it’s great to see a classic get a modern makeover, and the graphics are absolutely stunning. The environments are beautifully detailed, and navigating through the chaotic streets of Raccoon City can be nerve wrecking, especially with Nemesis right on your heels. 

However, it definitely feels like it’s missing something, especially for fans of the original. A lot of key moments and areas that made the first game so memorable are either shortened or cut entirely, which makes the whole game feel rushed. 

It’s clear that the developers wanted to create something special, but in the end, it feels like they sacrificed depth for a quicker experience. I wanted to be immersed in that terrifying world again, but instead, I felt like I was just skimming the surface. It’s fun, but it’s a missed chance to truly honor the original.

Overall, it’s definitely a fun experience for newcomers, but for fans of the original, it might not quite live up to expectations

I waited til I beat the game to write a review. Honestly, even after beating the game a few times, I didn't know what to write here. 

Pros.
Story is pretty similar to the original. There are noticeable differences, but overall, it's the same story I remember from the one I played as a kid. Graphics are nice without being a huge burden on the computer. Game play was ok. Not great, not terrible, just ok. Well made characters with facial expressions that fit the mood of the story. Not just the usual blinking eyes but full on facial expressions that look pretty realistic. You can see surprise, anger, relief, humor. Really nicely done. 

Cons.
Even though the story is similar, you can see A LOT of places where they cut things out. Not sure if it was to slim up the size of the game, or just to hurry it out the door and make money, but everything about it feels smaller and less engaging than the original. A lot of puzzles were cut out or reduced to go find this key which is pretty much in the room next door and come back and unlock this door. Early game seems to have a lot of back and forth and then nothing but a straight line. I miss the choices you could make when you encounter Nemesis. Depending on how you chose, you could drop him with background traps instead of having to face him every time. Which brings me to the next con. In the original, you only faced Nemesis a few times, and each time you would be given a choice in how to handle the encounter which could result in Nemesis being defeated for the time being and it was practically a guarantee that it would be a long while before you saw him again. This game cut content, cut out weapons, cut puzzles, only to push Nemesis on you every freaking step of the back and forth journey through this game. Add onto that the drastically reduced amount of ammo and gun powder you find, and it gets annoying really quickly. It just seems like it was a lazy attempt at a cash grab. If you are getting multiple achievements for completing the game in under 2 hours, and with the  slash to the types of weapons, gun powder, and puzzles that they cut out, it just seems to me like they just wanted to get this out the door as quickly and cheaply as possible, which is a shame, because the original was one of my all time favorite games. If you play this remake, and also play the RE2 remake, you can see a huge difference in the amount of effort that went into RE3. Where RE2 is recognizably a remake of the original with pretty much the same puzzles and the same layout as the original, and then you look at this game and understand how much was cut out, you can understand why I had trouble giving this a thumbs up. Yes it was fun. Was it as fun as it could have been if they had kept the same effort as the second remake? I don't think so. Yes, it had the same characters, and some of the story was recognizably RE3. Was the story as good with some of this missing stuff gone? I don't think so. Still, if you just treat it as its own game, and not think of it as a remake, then yeah it was ok. If you ask me if it's worth $60? No way. If you think about it, for the 2 hours of content you get, it should only be worth $20. 

I'm giving it a thumb up, just because it was somewhat fun to play even if it was short. Get it on sale for sure. Don't pay full price for 2 hours of cut content and missing weapons.

[h1]Resident Evil 3[/h1]
A streamlined, modern interpretation of the original Resident Evil 3; this rendition has faster gameplay, a more linear experience, and a heavier focus on cinematic cutscenes. It, however, lacks the terrifying atmospheric tension that the previous remake ever so well established, but that is not to diminish the thrill of action or chase sequences as well as significantly improved boss fights. The visual and audio fidelity remains astonishing, with additional improvements because of the utilization of Capcom's welcomed RE Engine.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The visuals have improved over RE2, not leaps and bounds by any means but improvements such as character models, facial expressions, and overall lighting. Everything remains thoroughly designed with attention to detail, from the design and creation to the texturing, lighting, and animation. It really shows via the characters, assets, and environments.

Exploration of the various streets and buildings within Raccoon City may not be as frightening as it was in RE2, but that is because of the fast-paced, action-orientated gameplay. That, however, does not diminish that the visuals alone still captivate that affection for Resident Evil and horror, resulting in unsettling and eerie surroundings regardless.

The zombies are visually terrifying and memorable alongside the plethora of other creatures and mutations which roam Raccoon City. The tyrant himself Nemesis, has a spectacular design that keeps on developing, with each encounter growing more ominous and disturbing still. Although it is not only the horrific beings that look great, as do the cast of characters you play and encounter. The models are unique and remarkable; the amount of care put into everybody, even the models you see once or twice, is unbelievable.

[h1]Audio[/h1]
Audibly it sounds great; the soundtrack is good and features some fun reimagined classic tracks from previous installments, alongside creating its new and reimagined score. The guns sound more realistic and satisfying than ever, which can also be said for the environment you are within, from sound effects like water droplets or footsteps to explosions; it all sounds astonishing.

Attention to detail is everywhere, especially when it comes to voice acting. With the cinematic narrative focus, it became crucial to nail the voice acting for the cast of characters, which Capcom did. Each character sounds splendid and has a voice befitting their personality and likeness, whether be it a grim or heartfelt moment, they always pull through and sound genuine. The groans and cries from Zombies still periodically send a chill down the spine. However, this is short-lived, as it is quickly quenched by satisfying death, after blowing the zombie's head.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
The traditional slow-paced action with great prominence on exploration has shifted to a more linear experience focusing on chase sequences, cinematic cutscenes, and much faster gunplay. While exploration does come into play, it feels shallow compared to the previous iteration. It will not be for everyone, especially veterans of the franchise. as it's at odds with the traditional free-roam, slow-paced survival horror that RE2 mastered.

The lack of puzzles, backtracking, areas to explore, and ultimately barely any incentive to scavenge are among the primary reasons exploration feels half-baked. Exploration will of course still reward additional upgrades, herbs, ammunition, and more if the player should explore. But due to the abundance of resources at hand, it never feels mandatory or incentivized.

Gunplay, however, feels fast, fluid, and most importantly fun. The addition of timed dodges allows combat to flow better and feel less clunky. Boss battles feel satisfying and well designed, as it's no longer simply. "run around the boss, and shoot it till it collapses." like in the previous installment.

I do firmly believe Capcom managed to design gameplay with a medium between Resident Evil and the more modern, fast-paced action formula quite well. It is by no means perfect, but it succeeds in staying enjoyable and distinct throughout the journey.

[h1]Story[/h1]
Following the events from Resident Evil 2, Raccoon City is still in chaos, as the virus is rampant, and victims of it arise as flesh-eating zombies that roam the streets. The story revolves around a S.T.A.R.S. member Jill Valentine as she tries to find a cure and figure out who created the virus and why while trying to escape the city with an imminent threat always around the corner. During this time, Jill encounters Carlos Oliveira, a member of the U.B.C.S who is tasked to lead the remaining civilians out of the city but ultimately gets entangled in Jill's journey.

The story is cheesy, albeit enjoyable, and certainly memorable; from the never-ending over-the-top action to the incredibly wholesome moments between Jill and Carlos, it all has personality and enjoyment written all over it. The villain, however, is forgettable, bland, and truly a missed opportunity to take the story to the next level.

[h1]Additional Note(s):[/h1]
Resident Evil 3 is bundled alongside Resident Evil Resistance, which is an asymmetric one versus four Multiplayer standalone game. It is, however, in a bad state as Capcom has abandoned it with no plans of fixing/updating it.

RE3 is a short game, as it's roughly 6-7 hours long with tons of content cut from the original. This fact is barely noticeable for newcomers, as what there is, feels like a solid enough experience. But for fans of the original game, it may feel underwhelming with so much left out, but ultimately still enjoyable, just something to keep in mind.

[h1] Final Thoughts [/h1]
Resident Evil 3 is a flawed yet enjoyable game that improves gunplay, making combat feel fluid and fast, but at the cost of the traditional slow-paced exploration-oriented gameplay and the atmospheric tension that the previous installment had mastered. It is visually and audibly stunning, with great characters, and has an enjoyable story only hindered by its villain. Despite its shortcomings, I do believe it is a good game, worthy of your time whether you are an RE fan or not.

[h1]Better than expected[/h1]

RE3 Remake got such negativity from the community that I avoided the game until now, when it finally dropped to a good price in an okay Halloween sale.  I still don't regret not buying it before, but upon playing it I was hugely surprised to find how good this title really is.

To put things in perspective: I've never thought OG RE3 was as good as people make it out to be. It was an okay game, like most Capcom output from that era, but to me it lacked something, it felt like a step back from OG RE2, which was an epic adventure with a compelling story, while Jill campaign had too small of a scope, was just too condensed, and the storywriters couldn't manage to even resemble the previous title in narrative structure, which involved a cast of memorable characters like Claire, Leon, Ada, Sherry, their parents etc. OG RE3 felt like a side episode instead of a numbered title (Code Veronica should have been RE 3, imo).

Having said that, it's obvious that I had zero expectations coming into this and was more open to new ideas and interpretations. First, I enjoyed Jill a lot in this. They just nailed her face model, her personality and expressions - she never appears as annoying as her competitor in the "single heroine carrying the game on her shoulders" department: the rebooted Lara Croft. In fact, Jill manages to show determination but still retaining a kind of charm, which neither modern Lara or Claire are able to do.
Then they get the pacing just right, and great pacing is the trademark of this series, perfected by RE1make and RE4 in their own way each, but also done amazingly well recently in RE7 and RE8. Important to note that pacing was not without flaws in RE2R, as shown by the weak sewer segment halting the flow of that game. This doesn't happen in Re3Remake, which goes along smoothly from beggining to end, with adrenaline pumping and fine tuned gameplay, cool (and some absurdly funny) setpieces, amazing models, animations and action choreography. The soundtrack is also spot on, and I thought it fared better on this game than the  one they composed for RE2R did.

What I must agree with the general opinion though, it's that they could have added more segments from the original. If we had a bit more content in the single player campaign, without hurting the pacing, this might have been the best of the new RE Engine games to me. As it stands, Village is the best from this modern bunch.

By the way, this review was written after completing a blind first playthough choosing Hardcore difficulty from the get go. I believe this is a great manner to experience these games.

Resident Evil 3 (1999) is and always will be my favorite Resident Evil game, and it's the first one we (me and my siblings) played when we were young, scared us senseless back then what with all that Nemesis chasing you around in a creepy infested city. 

This remake does bring back a lot of what was there in the original - the atmosphere and the monsters are still as eerie as ever, while improving on a lot of things like ofcourse the visuals and audio, cutscenes and characters etc, and then offer some new experiences with a faster paced over-the-shoulder gameplay. It's a really good game on it's own, but as it's a remake, we can't leave out the obvious - the missing pieces. The developers notoriously cut corners for some odd reason (maybe due to time constraints), they chose to remove two entire areas, several different Nemesis encounters, puzzles, a boss fight, a different ending and even an extra mini-game which had huge replayability value, these were elements that made the original such a fan favorite, this decision was really disappointing as it shortened the game by several hours. Given how good the game is at this state, those missing pieces would've made this a masterpiece.

Although it's a really botched remake, what we got here is still a really good game albeit a short one. If you played the original, and/or Resident Evil 2 remake, or any Resident Evil game in general, then you should definitely try this, the action alone is worth playing.

After the success (and personal admiration) of the Resident Evil 2 remake, I was extremely happy to hear that Resident Evil 3 was getting the same treatment. But after I finished the game and experienced all of its content (or the lack thereof), this is such a shallow imitation of the original PS1 release. In short, purchase the original RE3 on; PS1, PC or Gamecube. These have a lot more to offer than this "remake" (and are much cheaper).

Honestly, this will always be one of the biggest fumbles that Capcom has ever done in my book. I remember getting this game way back when it first came out on Xbox. My friends and I were very excited for this game as RE2's remake was phenomenal and thought it was going to be of the same quality. We were all pretty damn disappointed, especially as most of us in the party chat at the time had beaten or at least played the original release. Most of us were able to beat the game in a matter of hours, under 3 hours in one sitting in most cases. We were shocked at the short length of the game and felt ripped off. Upon revisiting the game recently I came away with those same feelings and 100%ing this game was a sad and disappointing chore.

Now, there are plenty of articles and videos and other reviews which go into excruciating detail about how horribly this release represents the story of RE3. I will not beat a dead horse here and waste anyone's time with a sermon, if you want to see how much we were robbed in detail the truth is out there. Glaring examples include the scripting of Nemesis, character assassination of Jill, omission of dynamic gameplay choices (go in the RPD station or stay and fight the monster), and personally the lack of the original Mercenaries mode. In short, the game is a hollow shell of the game it is meant to be a remake of. This game's omission of content and short run time genuinely have me feeling like this should have been DLC for RE2 remake. Crazy take, I know, but that is the feeling I got from this game. If they weren't going to put the effort in, why make the full game in the first place?

Now, apart from being a fan of the original game and hating how the story is represented here, I have to be honest with the gameplay itself. For all the narrative and thematic shortcomings this game has, I found zero performance issues with the game. From running it back at launch to running it on my desktop and Steam Deck (it works very well in handheld) the game ran absolutely fine. Zero bugs or frustrations to be had. Graphics were solid and the game looked great. This is to be expected as the work that went into RE2's remake set the stage for this release to be solid performance-wise. Just gotta be honest with this part at the very least.

Okay, time to sum this all up. If you like the original RE3 and care about stories and how characters are treated and portrayed you will come away from this one disappointed. If you simply want a Resident Evil flavored game which is essentially less than half of the game it is a remake of and simply want solid gameplay and a short story, you can find enjoyment here. This is truly one of the games of all time, I would probably have enjoyed it a lot better if it wasn't claiming to be a remake of RE3. This game is a solid (and charitable) 5/10 and is truly a prominent example of wasted potential, especially given how amazing RE2 and RE4's remakes were.

As a long-time fan of the Resident Evil franchise, it's safe to say I’ve experienced nearly every entry — from the absolute masterpieces like Resident Evil 4 to the more divisive titles like RE5 and RE6. I’ve loved them all in some way, shape, or form. Heck, even Resident Evil 7 was a welcome shift in style. I’m still looking forward to diving into the remakes of Resident Evil 2, Resident Evil 4, and Resident Evil 8, but there’s one title that’s always stood out to me: Resident Evil 3: Nemesis.

For newcomers to the series or those who never played the original Resident Evil 3, this remake is perfectly serviceable. It’s an action-packed ride with little downtime, which might appeal to fans of fast-paced gameplay. The chase sequences with Nemesis are intense and frequent, and the game never feels too slow. If you’re coming into this fresh, you might have a good time.

However, if you’ve played the original RE3 — or if you’ve come to love its slower, more atmospheric tension — the changes in this remake might leave you disappointed. The game feels short — far shorter than the original, which had more breathing room and a greater sense of exploration. Here, the focus is almost entirely on action and Nemesis chases, which leaves very little room for the puzzles, character interactions, and environmental storytelling that made the original stand out.

One of the most frustrating aspects of the remake is how much content was cut. The original RE3 had more variety in its pacing. There were sections where you could take your time solving puzzles, exploring, and interacting with other characters. The remake trims all of this down, opting instead to ramp up the action. This works for some, but for me, it took away what made the original so special — the balance between survival horror, exploration, and action.

The plot changes also stood out to me as a major flaw. While it’s not uncommon for remakes to take liberties with story elements, some of the decisions here felt like missed opportunities. For example, the death of Brad Vickers, a moment that was genuinely shocking and impactful in the original, barely registers here. Similarly, the iconic Barry Burton appearance at the end is gone, which is another change that felt like a misstep. There are more plot deviations, but I won’t spoil them here. Suffice to say, for long-time fans of the original, these changes can feel jarring.

Looking at the overwhelmingly “Very Positive” reviews on Steam, I get the impression that many players are enjoying the game in isolation, without comparing it to its predecessor. That’s fine, and I can understand why people are giving it high marks. It’s not a bad game, just a mediocre one when stacked against the original. It’s certainly fun in parts, but it’s also a missed opportunity. For fans who grew up with the original RE3, the remake feels more like a fast-paced action game with a few elements tacked on rather than a faithful reimagining.

In the end, I’m going to give the game a positive review as well — maybe not as glowing as some others, but it’s still a fun time, especially if you’re not attached to the original. But, for me, it’s hard to shake the feeling that Resident Evil 3: Nemesis deserved more than just a straightforward action reboot.

Despite its short duration, Resident Evil 3 delivers an intense and fast-paced experience that lingers even after completion.

From the very first minute, the game plunges you into the midst of Raccoon City's collapse, never allowing you a moment's respite. Burning buildings, sirens, dark streets… everything is so well-designed that not only progressing but even feeling the environment becomes part of the game. The atmosphere constantly creates pressure, and this feeling never disappears throughout the game.

Jill Valentine carries the story with her strong stance and determination. Her ability to maintain control even amidst the chaos makes her character even more compelling. On the other hand, the sections played as Carlos Oliveira add a different tempo to the game. Carlos's more action-oriented gameplay and perspective save the story from monotony and offer a richer experience.

Nemesis is the game's greatest signature. Not just a powerful enemy, but also a constant source of pressure. The unpredictable timing of his appearance and the challenges he poses in every encounter keep the tension at a constant level. The chase scenes, in particular, are truly adrenaline-pumping.

In terms of gameplay, the game offers a faster-paced and action-oriented structure. While this deviates somewhat from the classic Resident Evil atmosphere, it significantly improves the fluidity. You're constantly on the move, you have to make decisions, and this keeps the game from becoming boring.

On the criticism side, the biggest drawback is definitely its length. Just when you're fully immersed in the game, it can feel like it ends a little too soon. Some players might wish for more detailed exploration of certain sections. However, despite this, the experience it offers is so intense that you don't feel any emptiness while playing.

In short:
Resident Evil 3, despite its debatable length, offers an unforgettable experience with its atmosphere, pace, and character variety. If you're looking for a short but impactful game, it's definitely worth a try.

Resident Evil 3 is a remake of the game that was originally released in 1999, where the tank controls and fixed camera angles have been replaced with a modern control scheme and a third person camera perspective. 

I never played the original version, so my review will judge this like a new game, rather than comparing it to the old one. I’ve played most of the other Resident Evil games though (this is my 10th RE game) and speaking as a fan of the franchise, I mostly enjoyed RE3.

[h1]The Good[/h1]

•	The main playable character is Jill Valentine, but you’ll also control Carlos Oliveira during a couple of missions.

•	Weapons include knife, pistol, shotgun, grenade launcher (which has four different types of ammo), assault rifle and magnum, as well as throwable grenades and flashbangs.

•	There are a few different enemies including zombies, dogs, hunters, a strange lizard monster, and then there’s the Nemesis who shows up at various times for some tough boss fights.

•	Ammo and healing supplies are limited, so you need to manage your resources carefully. The level design is quite linear with not much opportunity to just run past enemies, so its important to have good aim to not waste bullets. There was one boss fight near the end of the game that I won with my last shotgun shell.

•	There are a couple of basic puzzles to solve to find extra items or weapon upgrades. You can use gunpowder and explosives to craft different ammo types, which was especially useful for me because I didn’t actually find the magnum during my playthrough, so instead of giving me ammo that I couldn’t use, I was able to craft ammo for the guns I did have.

•	Story is on the same quality level as most RE games (in other words, “fine”), but the cutscenes are exciting and voice acting for Jill and Carlos is great.

•	Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard.

•	Graphics look fantastic. I didn’t encounter any bugs or crashes and I had a perfectly smooth framerate throughout.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]

•	It took me just over 7 hours to complete, which isn’t good value for the £50 price. Lots of other reviews have mentioned that some content from the original version has been cut out of this remake, which is a shame because if they’d included everything I think it could have solved the biggest complaint.

•	Okay, the £50 also includes the Resistance multiplayer mode, but I’ve watched gameplay footage on youtube and it looks really bad. There’s no way I’d consider playing it instead of my preferred multiplayer games, so that doesn’t add any value for me.

[h1]The Recommendation[/h1]

The gameplay of Resident Evil 3 is really enjoyable, I just wish there was more of it. Wait for a 50% sale or better.

It begins with fire. Not the kind that warms — the kind that devours.

The city screams in sirens and smoke. Ash sticks to your skin. Streets you once knew twist into something unrecognizable, swallowed by panic and rot. The world feels like it’s ending — not with silence, but with teeth.

People run, but not fast enough. Doors slam, barricades fall, voices fade. Infection spreads like a whisper passed from hand to hand, and suddenly everything familiar turns hostile.

But the worst part isn’t the chaos.
It’s the rhythm.
The sound that doesn’t stop.
The footsteps.

Measured. Heavy. Inevitable.

You run until your lungs burn, and still — it’s behind you. Not hunting for food. Not for revenge. Just… to end you.

Walls collapse. Creatures claw through the dark. Streets become labyrinths of debris and blood. You keep moving, not because you’re brave, but because stopping means becoming part of the rubble.

Weapons buy you seconds, not safety. Choices feel like coin flips made in fire. And through it all, that sound returns: those steps, like a countdown you can’t reset.

But something awakens inside you. A refusal. A flicker of fight buried beneath the fear. You slam a door. You fire a shot. You scream not because you’re afraid — but because you’re still alive.

And maybe, just maybe, survival isn’t about escaping what chases you.

Maybe it’s about proving that no matter how monstrous the world becomes — there’s still someone in the rubble who refuses to break.

The number of areas that were removed from the original game alongside their respective puzzles is enormous.

The recreated personality of Jill is awful (and for many people, her recreated appearence too). Capcom had a great opportunity to create an incredible and cherished remake, even more than RE 2, but instead has created a huge disappointment for much of its fanbase and showed how greedly rushed the Remake was.

[h1]Resident Evil 3 (2020)[/h1]

[i]Resident Evil 3[/i], the great remake that could have been. I was one of the fools who pre-ordered this game on PS4 thinking it was going to be bigger than RE2R. For someone who holds RE3 Nemesis as one of my top RE games, I have a lot to say here.

To make things clear: as an action horror game, it's [b]okay[/b]; there are issues here and there but it works about 80% of the time at least. As a Resident Evil game AND a Resident Evil remake, it's pretty terrible. There are a couple of ways to tackle this game so I'll be reviewing it from the perspective of one who's grown up playing the original 1999 game.

That being said, this is probably my least favorite RE game and I didn't have that much more fun outside of my first playthrough.

[u]Story + Characters (Possible Spoilers!)[/u]

[spoiler]Most people will mention a lot about how improved the storyline is in the remake compared to RE3 Nemesis and I can see why: it's a lot more focused and streamlined. The plot for RE3R is almost like the original plot, except there's a plotline switch that focuses from escaping the city to getting the vaccine to stop the missile strike from blowing up... Raccoon City?[/spoiler]

[spoiler]The issue I have with this story is that, halfway, it goes absolutely nowhere. Jill makes the vaccine to "save the city" and the vaccine gets destroyed anyway (Jill couldn't care less about RC at the end). Also, aside from other reasons, Jill already has the T-virus antibodies from being cured so this plotline with the vaccine was pointless.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]It's like the RE3R team read a synopsis of the RE3 plot and decided it needed a human main antagonist to show that, "oh, it's not the monsters that are actual evil, it's human greed that's actual evil" except the original already showed these points much better without Nicholai being such a blatant villain with actual subtlety.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]As for the characters, almost everyone in this game has been dumbed down to a certain degree. Jill is snobby and acts way too hard to be a badass, Nicholai may as well be wearing a big white mustache to twirl whenever he's going to do something evil, Mikhail's despair over the loss of his subordinates under him is replaced by a generic disgruntled leader character, Dario is turned from a survivor struck with overwhelming grief over his daughter's death to a complete noodle of an idiot, and Nemesis is turned into an incompetent goofball that only tosses Jill around even when he's got her dead to rights. The only characters who improved from the original were Tyrell and Carlos who is by far the best character out of everyone; anyone who plays this game will LOVE Carlos.[/spoiler]

[u]Gameplay[/u]

This game is [b]short[/b]. That could be confusing considering that most RE games are short, but RE3R is one of the shortest Resident Evil games I've ever played due to the fact that it's the [i]most[/i] linear RE game yet. The reason for why this game can be completed so quickly is that there's not really much to explore compared to other RE games; you never have to backtrack that much because what you leave behind is relatively insignificant and you never have to go back to places for more puzzle solving. My first run was a little under three hours on PS4 and I explored as much as I could.

Given that the gameplay is derived from RE2R, it's still solid. Aiming and shooting feels good, controls are responsive, dodging is fun to do but is situational because enemies will sometimes rush you down from behind which makes dodging based on luck at that point. However, that's basically all there is to say that is good about the gameplay because the pacing that this game goes at does not work with the mechanics. 

Many new enemies you meet are either long ranged or agile which results in you trying to spin your camera to see where they're at and attempting to dodge them. They also range from being insignificant to defeat or being outright drivel. Ne-α Parasites can hit you from nearly across an entire room, Drain Deimos are relegated to one section and are never seen again, Hunter Gammas are almost free enemies considering that one shotgun blast to their mouths stuns them and one Flame Round will kill them, Pale Heads are lazily reused from RE2R's Ghost Survivors, and Hunter Betas are armored and can now randomly one-shot you at ANY condition of health with almost no warning. Dispatching enemies is easy because the game will give you the resources right next to the enemy that is weak to it ([spoiler]example, the Sewer section[/spoiler]) and you are given so much ammo in this game even on harder difficulties.

Nemesis T-Type is the titular enemy that made RE3 Nemesis as memorable as it was. Although he's much stronger than any enemy you will encounter, compared to his original, he is an absolute joke. Mind you, this was basically Umbrella's peak tyrant who could tank 10 Freeze Rounds, take two Rocket Launcher missiles, three Red Barrels, and would still come after you 11 times in the original AND follow you in most areas of the Raccoon City streets. In the Remake, up to Hardcore difficulty, a single Hand Grenade or Red Barrel can down him the fastest. Nemesis only ever truly stalks you in the Downtown area once ([spoiler]after the Power Station[/spoiler]). For him to be anywhere as tough, you basically have to amp up the difficulty to the point where his attack patterns become unfair ([spoiler]final boss, anyone?[/spoiler]).

There is no reason to think about item management at all. There are few key items that are used to progress forward and those that you do get are quickly / twice used (at most) to progress because it's so obvious where to use them. Puzzles are laughably easy to complete (with one puzzle at the end requiring a tiny bit of thought) and are almost non-existent; most "puzzles" that require you to progress will simply be installing key items, unlocking doors, or turning on switches.

It's never a good sign when there are challenges in a Resident Evil game that make you grind hundreds of kills in a series that EMPHASIZES on saving resources, running past a majority of enemies, and killing only what you're required to especially in an action horror game as short as this one. After beating the game, you're left with playing the game on harder difficulties and completing records to unlock rewards, but the replay value is short; I was able to 100% the game within a [b]day and a half[/b].

[u]Graphics & Sound[/u]

I will admit at least that the graphics on RE3R are as beautiful as usual for a game that uses the RE engine. However, I couldn't help but feel that RE2R had much better use of shadows and gore to emphasize the horror aspect and rarely was I ever tense playing this game. Many of the character designs are great; I liked Carlos' design the best and Jill's design is good enough for people to make mods for her.

The sound effects for the guns, explosions, and the chaos of the city are decent as well. Nothing sounded out of place or as if I was shooting out anything weaker or stronger than what the gun looked like.

[u]Conclusion[/u]

Like everyone else mentions, there's an insane amount of cut OG content. In short, about 70% of RE3 has either been changed or outright cut from the remake. To name a few: no Enhanced Ammo, no Clock Tower, no Park, no Cemetery, no Incineration Disposal Plant, no Grave Diggers or Brain Suckers, no complex mixing of Gunpowders and Grenades, no Nemesis-dropped weapons like the STI EAGLE.

It's a damn shame because newer fans will never know how much better this game could have been. Such aspects matter if taking them out removes a lot of depth from the remake and given how easy it is to complete this game in under an hour without speedrun strats, it only goes to show. I would only buy this game on discount and would recommend to RE fans just so you can say you've played it.

So having JUST finished playing the game for the first time (haven't done any replays yet as of this writing), I must say... Resident Evil 3 Remake ended up being a big letdown for me in the end. I still had enough fun playing the game to finish it without it feeling like a chore to do so, and to be fair the game definitely HAS a few good things going for it (good soundtrack, immersive-looking world, a couple tweaks to some of RE2R's gameplay mechanics such as removing knife durability and adding a dodge mechanic that feels better than the original RE3's, and a couple good tension-inducing set-pieces such as the substation and several of the early in-game Nemesis chases, to name a couple examples), but sitting here reviewing the entire package now that I'm done playing it, my first impressions of the entire thing are mixed to negative, especially when viewing it as a remake of Resident Evil 3: Nemesis. 

In a nutshell, as a game that serves as a follow-up to Resident Evil 2 Remake I feel it's a letdown that doesn't measure up to it's overall more-polished predecessor, even if I admit the game is arguably fun enough on it's own depending on your mindset when playing the game... as a GAME. It's not a bad game to PLAY by any stretch, but it's a definite downgrade to everything the developers of RE2R had going for THEIR game, which still managed to keep most of the soul of the original RE2 as a survival horror game where you explore several complex, isolated locations with limited resources intact... which is more than I can say for RE3R, which on the whole feels closer to being a toned-down version of RE6 with an altered, compressed version of RE3's story than it does the original RE3, a game which cranked up the action from the original RE2 but was still at it's core a classic survival horror game similar to it's predecessor back in the day, albeit in a more open world (for the first half of that game, at least). 

Now, as a REMAKE of Resident Evil 3: Nemesis for the PlayStation 1... RE3R was simply awful. There's so much wrong with it in this respect that I feel that I could easily make my own dedicated video on the subject comparing this remake to the original on just this aspect alone, if I really wanted to. A short summary of things that come to the top of my mind, as of me having just finished the game, are as follows: Half the original game's content is missing (no clock tower, park, Dead Factory, most of Raccoon City's streets and buildings you get to explore are gone, no construction zone, the Gravedigger boss is completely gone, etc., etc..), a good bit of what DOES remain story/content-wise has been changed up in ways that feels inferior to the original more often than not, the changes in characterization feels like a mixed bag across the board (I do NOT like the changes to Jill and Nikolai's characters in this game, while everyone else I'm either neutral on or have no particular preference when compared to their original counterparts. Brad is the only character whose changed characterization I actually feel is an overall improvement from his original portrayal), the choice mechanic from the original game that influences how the story/game progressed is entirely absent (which was the source of most of the original RE3's replayability, but not here - apparently you play through RE3R once and you've already experienced everything the game's story has to offer), and they reduce the titular monster of the original game into a joke compared to his original incarnation -- one that the other characters treat more as an annoyance than a serious deadly threat to be feared (he isn't reduced to a joke in just story, either -- for most part he's been made into a joke during gameplay, too -- he's far less difficult than he was in the original game overall.). I'm just sitting here amazed at how much this game utterly failed to not only live up to my expectations as a follow-up to RE2R, but especially as a remake to one of my favorite games in the series. 

The game was arguably at it's best during the first 1/4, maybe a bit beyond that -- but once I defeated the Nemesis in his first actual boss battle, it seems like the overall quality of the game started to take a nosedive and kept going down all the way until the credits started to roll... which makes it quite frustrating for me because for that first quarter of the game I felt that I could see little hints of what this game COULD have been like if it had been given some more polish, but unfortunately a world where we got a remake of RE3 with a similar level of polish to the RE2 Remake is NOT the world we're living in right now.

So in conclusion, I'd recommend anyone who's looking into getting into the Resident Evil series to stick to the original game and avoid this remake -- the original is a far better game overall than this remake is, IMO. But if you absolutely MUST try this game for yourself, then get it on sale because I don't think RE3R has enough going for it to justify paying for it full-price... and even then I would STILL avoid playing it until AFTER you've played through the original Resident Evil 3 shortly beforehand, so that way you can experience all the differences from the original game for yourselves. But if you choose to think of and play RE3R as just a follow-up to RE2R instead of comparing it to the original game, then while it certainly could be a lot better... you could also do a lot worse than RE3R.

Resident Evil 3 takes a more action oriented approach compared to its predecessor, much like the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis did within the classic trilogy. However, even among those older titles, Nemesis was arguably the weakest entry, and unfortunately, this modern remake doesn't manage to elevate its source material in a meaningful way. In fact, it not only falls short as a remake but also struggles to uphold the identity of a Resident Evil game.

Like the Resident Evil 2 Remake, it's not a one to one recreation. It is more like a reimagining with considerable creative liberties, not all of which work in its favor. While some of the original's core ideas are still present, they have been altered in ways that make the game feel more like a cinematic action thriller than a survival horror game. There's a clear emphasis on cutscenes, dialogue, and scripted moments, which gives the game a more "movie like" quality but at the expense of player agency and atmospheric tension.

Visually, there's little to complain about. The RE Engine continues to impress, with highly detailed environments, excellent character models, and realistic facial animations. Zombies, although largely recycled from Resident Evil 2, still look convincing. From a technical standpoint, the game is well produced. But gameplaywise it moves the game further away from its survival horror roots.

Nemesis, the big bad thing you already see on the covers, should have been a standout feature. In the original, his encounters were tense, unpredictable, and often dynamic. Here, he is reduced to a mostly scripted presence. His initial appearance in the city streets is arguably the highlight of the game one of the few moments that captures the chaotic energy of the original. But subsequent encounters are heavily controlled and lack tension. His mutations are less grotesque and feel disconnected from the biological horror that once made him terrifying. Instead of evolving in response to the player's actions, his transformations now follow a fixed, cinematic path, turning him into a quadruped like creature that's visually odd rather than intimidating. It's strange, with the Tyrant from Resident Evil 2, they've already introduced an enemy into the series who has somehow evolved from the original. But here, it really seems to be the case that Nemesis is even better in the original than he is in the remake.

Also Carlos, a side character from the original, plays a much larger role in the remake. His expanded sections include new locations and extended gameplay time sometimes even replacing segments originally played with Jill. While his improved presence could have added depth, these sections often feel more like a generic third person shooter. Armed with an assault rifle and abundant ammunition, Carlos storms through waves of zombies, holding out against dozens of them in a sequence that feels more like a scripted shooter scenario than a survival horror game. It was similar in the original, but here they could go on a different road, instead of making everything more over the top.

Equally disappointing is the removal or truncation of key areas from the original. The clock tower and parts of the factory are missing entirely, and some of the game's characters are introduced so briefly that they leave no lasting impression. The Mercenaries mode has also been cut, and puzzles once a staple of the series have been either removed or simplified to such a degree that they no longer offer any meaningful challenge. You get Resident Evil Resistence instead, a stand alone multiplayer game nobody asked for.

Unfortunately, combat often feels unsatisfying. Zombies are unusually durable, absorbing bullets unpredictably. The game doesn't encourage careful aiming or offer consistent feedback for well placed shots. Critical hits seem to occur at random rather than as a reward for skill. Boss fights are similarly unengaging, typically resolved by unloading the most powerful weapons until the enemy collapses. There's little strategy involved, and these encounters rarely evolve beyond their visual spectacle. The new dodge roll require also less precise timing and makes them far more forgiving and with full control over aiming and movement, there's little reason to flee one of the core survival instincts that the older games used to evoke. An engaging, although immensely flawed "remake" of the PS1 classic. 

How does RE3R compare to its original counterpart?
-No more choices/diverging paths/only one ending.
-Less Nemesis encounters/he's easier to take down/has disappointing drop supplies.
-Less weapons, costumes and overall unlockables.
-Mercenaries mode replaced by an inferior Dead by Daylight-esque "Resistance" multiplayer.

Despite all its faults, RE3R is one of my favorite modern entries in the series. The dodge mechanic is smoother and more rewarding than it felt in the original. Knife-only runs are a blast, especially after unlocking the Hot Dogger. The visuals are outstanding and everything plays out like a movie. While physically different from their classic counterparts, Jill and Carlos are still charming and likable protagonists. The story more or less follows the original's structure, with some changes here and there (ex. Tyrell has more screen time and Brad has a different fate). The writing is nothing special, but it's concise and to the point. There are plenty of interesting files to read; anyone into the series' lore won't be let down. RE3R also has an active modding community, thereby any issues (regarding the characters' looks and so forth) have plenty of fixes.

Been a huge RE fan since 1998, and will always defend the classic fixed camera games. I sympathize with anyone who may be disappointed with RE3R, being a fan of the original myself. But I've considered the production issues which played a role in RE3R's faults. For one thing, Capcom wasted resources focusing on its accompanying multiplayer, when they could have spent more time expanding the campaign itself. RE3R was also developed between RE2R and RE8, the latter which promises to have more replayability, as RE2R did. With these thoughts in mind, I must give credit where credit is due. Even with its short length and missing content,  RE3R is still fun with what the development team were able to achieve.     

Again, the problem with RE3R isn't so much what's in the game, but what's missing. Just as the game reaches its peak it ends. It's unfortunate, although I still recommend RE3R (especially on discount) to anyone who enjoys zombie media and modern RE.
